headline: High: OpenHands can write/execute broadly while Copilot can modify repo state, creating dangerous default interaction paths for leakage, conflicts, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Copilot reads repo context and open editor buffers, while OpenHands can operate on mounted files and MCP-backed inputs. A malicious file or prompt in shared workspace can influence Copilot’s suggestions and then be consumed by OpenHands. The shared-file pathway is plausible, though not proven to be default across both runtimes.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same repository or mounted workspace
IF OpenHands ingests Copilot-authored text as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate workspaces for the two agents
Disable automatic acceptance of Copilot-generated edits
Add a manual review step before OpenHands acts on any text from Copilot
Use provenance labels in shared files
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization or instruction-stripping between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Copilot touches source code and open buffers and sends requests to api.githubcopilot.com; OpenHands reads files in its runtime and can use broad network egress. If sensitive files are mounted into OpenHands or opened in Copilot buffers, both can expose the same data class through different backends. The shared-workspace path is plausible, but not enough evidence for a higher severity.
conditions: IF sensitive files are present in the repo or runtime mount
IF OpenHands or Copilot is allowed to transmit those files to its backend
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared repo and runtime mount
Use redacted fixtures for agent tasks
Restrict OpenHands network access to approved endpoints
Review Copilot and OpenHands logs for sensitive strings
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem and modify git state. Copilot Workspace proposes edits for human review, while OpenHands executes actions inside a runtime sandbox and can also write and commit. If they target the same repo or mounted volume, concurrent writes and git-state changes can overwrite each other or corrupt work. The overlap is explicit in both profiles.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository checkout or mounted volume
IF either agent writes or commits without external locking
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate branch
Pause one agent while the other writes
Use file-level locks on shared paths
Require human approval before git commits
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: Copilot produces edits and suggestions that OpenHands can treat as actionable workspace content, while OpenHands has shell, browser, and subprocess authority. That creates a default pathway where one agent’s output becomes the other’s input and then becomes real actions without strong verification. The blast radius includes incorrect code changes or unsafe runtime actions.
conditions: IF OpenHands consumes Copilot-generated edits or text as authoritative
IF no independent verification step checks the proposed changes before execution
mitigations: Require a second human review before execution
Compare proposed diffs against tests before applying them
Disable autonomous action execution for shared tasks
Limit OpenHands to read-only analysis on Copilot-produced files
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: Copilot is tied to GitHub repo context and vendor APIs, while OpenHands runs in a Docker runtime and may use remote runtimes or configured model-provider APIs. If regulated data is placed in the shared repo or runtime, differing retention and residency assumptions can create compliance mismatch. The profiles do not prove a specific regime, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared repository or runtime mount
IF the configured OpenHands model provider or Copilot service retains prompts beyond policy
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared agent tasks
Use synthetic or masked datasets
Confirm retention settings for both services
Document residency and DPA coverage before use
requires-engineering: route regulated workloads to compliant deployments
